segments.text: Part of what made this round of tornadoes in and around Oklahoma City, particularly terrifying,
was that thousands of families were trapped in their cars, traffic coming to a standstill on major
highways with that storm brewing. Closer the gridlock proving deadly in the end of course,
this happened right around the rush hour. Many family said they'd been told to try to flee the storms.
ABC's Alex Perez also in Oklahoma tonight on that part of the story.
With the deadly tornado looming above, a driver's nightmare was unfolding below. Complete gridlock
along Interstate 40 and roadways across central Oklahoma. You look at it on TV and you see it coming
and you say, that's it, I'm leaving. I'm not going to wait around another second for this one.
Beverly L. Lam is one of thousands who panicked and got on the road trying to escape the twister's
path. Problem is she drove right into what seemed like a parking lot. We thought we had more time
and weren't expecting this mass exodus of people coming out and as we turned and got out into a
line, then we realized it was just bumper to bumper and gridlock. And as she peered out the back
window, she snapped his pick with her iPhone, the storm now right behind her. It's really approaching
you faster than you can get away from it. Then you start to get a little frightened. Many were
torn by conflicting messages. Some local media urge residents to get in their cars and flee south.
I think the reason for this is because May 20th is still, as I've said, is just very much still in
our hearts and minds. And this is too much too soon and we didn't expect this at all. And I think
it instilled a little bit of paranoia in people. But that paranoia led to a traffic standstill and
proved deadly, nine killed. Alam ended up driving to a nearby convenience store and seeking shelter
in a freezer with several others. But Oklahoma City Mayor Mick Cornett scolding those residents
who took to the roads. They should have known better. They'd had two or three days to know this
storm was likely. Wow, some tough words there from the mayor, particularly given how jittery everyone
was after having survived just a week ago what happened. Then the storms were turning. But Alex,
you reached out to the National Weather Service today. What are you supposed to do? Are you ever
supposed to flee a storm in your car? Well, David, the National Weather Service says you should
never get in your car and try to flee a tornado unless you have several hours to get ahead of it.
Now they say if you are already in your car and cannot get to somewhere safe, you should move your
car away from traffic lanes and put your seatbelt on and make sure your head is beneath the windows.
But of course, the first line of defense is always to try to get to a shelter like our friend Beverly
did. And of course, the reminder again, never try to get in your car and escape a tornado unless you
have several hours to work with.
